Need To Know
US Flights Resume
US commercial flight operations are
expected to return to normal
today after Friday’s ground stop scrambled travel throughout the weekend. Of the flights that departed yesterday morning, around 90% left within 14 minutes of their scheduled time.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy cited a newly installed router at a remote FAA facility in Arkansas as a factor in the disruption. A contractor installed the router while replacing old copper wire with
fiber-optic cable (
why are fiber-optic
cables better
?). The router then sent thousands of connection requests every few seconds to other routers across the network, disrupting communications at 17 of the FAA’s 22 air route traffic control centers. The incident renewed attention to the FAA’s aging infrastructure; Duffy
called on Congress
to approve an additional $50B in funding to modernize the nation’s air traffic control systems.
A 2025 report estimated that aviation infrastructure needs $114B more than projected funding will cover over the next decade (see graphic of America’s
infrastructure funding gap
Bahrain Base Attack
Iran attacked Bahrain for the
second time in days
yesterday, targeting a US air defense radar system at Bahrain’s Riffa Air Base. The attack followed Friday’s announcement by the US that it had intercepted two drones targeting Bahrain.
The US says neither attack caused known damage or injuries, though Iran maintains Friday’s attack struck the US’ early-warning radar system. Iran says it was a response to recent US strikes, including the Nov. 2 attack on
Qeshm Island
. The rate of strikes between the US and Iran has slowed in recent months; however, President Donald Trump has threatened to ramp up its military offensive, saying the US has “one or two” targets left (which may include
Pickaxe Mountain
). He has, meanwhile, publicly downplayed the value of a diplomatic resolution, pulling Vice President JD Vance off the US-Iran negotiations team and highlighting the US’
economic pressure tactics

Reduce, Reuse, Relaunch
SpaceX’s launch tower
caught the upper stage
of its Starship rocket for the first time Saturday after the nearly 171-foot-long spacecraft returned from orbit. The midair retrieval marks a milestone toward the company’s goal of building reusable rockets.
Starship spent roughly 22 hours in orbit, completing 14 trips around Earth before returning to the tower in South Texas. Two mechanical arms attached to the tower caught the spacecraft as it descended. Watch the historic landing
here
SpaceX previously used the system to catch Starship’s lower booster, but Saturday marked the first successful catch of the upper stage. Unlike the company’s Falcon 9 rockets, whose upper stages are discarded after launch, Starship was designed to be reusable. During Friday’s test flight, the lower booster did not return to the tower and instead splashed down in the Gulf.
Since its founding in 2002, SpaceX has conducted over 700 rocket launches. Watch a three-minute explanation of how Elon Musk built the company
